key_terms.term: Distributed parameters R, L, G, C
key_terms.meaning: Resistance, inductance, conductance and capacitance per metre of line; they replace lumped values when the line is longer than a fraction of a wavelength.
∂v/∂z = −Ri − L ∂i/∂t and ∂i/∂z = −Gv − C ∂v/∂t, the two coupled equations that describe voltage and current along a line.
Z₀ = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC)) Ω; for a lossless line it reduces to √(L/C).
γ = α + jβ = √((R + jωL)(G + jωC)); α in Np/m sets loss, β in rad/m sets phase.
A line with R/L = G/C, so α is flat and vp = 1/√(LC) is the same for all frequencies and the pulse shape is preserved.
vp = ω/β = λf, the speed at which a single frequency's phase travels down the line.
Γ = (Z<sub>L</sub> − Z₀)/(Z<sub>L</sub> + Z₀), a complex number giving the amplitude and phase of the wave sent back by the load.
Voltage standing wave ratio S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage on a mismatched line.
Return loss = −20 log₁₀|Γ| dB; a large value means little power comes back.
The fixed pattern of voltage maxima and minima produced when a forward and a reflected wave of the same frequency add.
ML = −10 log₁₀(1 − |Γ|²) dB, how far the delivered power is below the incident power; 0.97 dB for |Γ| = 0.447.
Z<sub>in</sub> = Z₀(Z<sub>L</sub> + jZ₀ tan βl)/(Z₀ + jZ<sub>L</sub> tan βl), the impedance seen at distance l from the load.
Line length measured in radians or degrees, βl = 2πl/λ; it decides how a load is transformed.
A λ/4 section of impedance Z₀′ = √(Z₀ Z<sub>L</sub>) that turns a real load into a match at one frequency.
Stub at d where Re Y(d) = Y₀, sized to cancel B(d); tan βd = [XL ± √(RL((Z₀ − RL)² + XL²)/Z₀)]/(RL − Z₀).
A shorted or open line section of length ls placed in parallel or series to cancel the load reactance so the input looks like Z₀.
A polar plot of Γ on which normalized impedance and admittance circles turn matching into a ruler-and-compass construction.
The permittivity a printed line behaves as if it had, because its field is split between substrate and air.
The lowest frequency at which a waveguide mode propagates; below fc the wave decays and carries no real power.
λg = 2π/β = λ₀/√(1 − (fc/f)²), the spacing between phase fronts inside the guide.
vp = c/√(1 − (fc/f)²) and vg = c√(1 − (fc/f)²) in an air guide; vp·vg = c².
The lowest-order rectangular-waveguide mode, with fc = c/(2a) for broad wall a; the usual working mode.
Q = ω₀ × (energy stored)/(power lost) = f₀/BW; it sets how sharp a resonator's response is.
1/QL = 1/Q₀ + 1/Qe; g = Q₀/Qe: g = 1 is critical coupling, g > 1 overcoupled.

takeaways: A transmission line is described completely by four per-metre quantities, and from them Z₀, α, β and vp follow.
When R/L equals G/C the line is distortionless, so attenuation is flat and a pulse keeps its shape.
Any load mismatch sends back a wave; Γ measures it, S and return loss report it, and both are read directly from |Γ|.
Input impedance depends on load and electrical length, so a short looks like an inductor, an open like a capacitor, and a λ/2 section repeats the load.
A quarter-wave transformer matches a real load only near one frequency, while a stub cancels reactance at a chosen point on the line.
The Smith chart is just the Γ plane with impedance circles drawn on it, so every matching step is a rotation and a circle crossing.
Printed lines such as microstrip and stripline trade compactness and easy fabrication against loss and radiation, with ε_eff setting Z₀ and λ.
A hollow waveguide passes a mode only above its cutoff, and the mode indices plus the metal dimensions fix fc, λg and vp.
A resonator's Q ties stored energy to loss; higher Q means a narrower bandwidth and a longer ring-down time.
Matching buys power transfer and low reflection, but every matching network has a finite bandwidth that must be checked.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine a derivation of the line equations with a numerical impedance, matching or waveguide calculation, and ask you to justify the choice between coax, printed line and waveguide for a given band. Every model answer below ends with a numerical check.

bank.q: Define the distributed parameters of a transmission line and derive the telegrapher's equations from a short element of length Δz. Solve them for a sinusoidal source to obtain Z₀ and γ.
outline: Draw the element with series RΔz, LΔz and shunt GΔz, CΔz
Apply KVL round the series path and KCL at the shunt node, divide by Δz, let Δz → 0
Write the two first-order equations; differentiate to get second-order wave equations
Assume V = V₀e<sup>−γz</sup> and state γ = α + jβ = √((R + jωL)(G + jωC))
State Z₀ = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC)) and the lossless limits √(L/C) and β = ω√(LC)
Give units: R, L, G, C per metre; α in Np/m, β in rad/m, Z₀ in ohms
answer: Distributed parameters. A line is two conductors whose length is comparable with the wavelength, so its resistance, inductance, leakage and capacitance are spread along it. Per metre they are R (Ω/m, metal resistance), L (H/m, magnetic field around the conductors), G (S/m, leakage through the dielectric) and C (F/m, electric field between the conductors).

answer.text: Model a slice of length Δz as series RΔz and LΔz followed by shunt GΔz and CΔz, with voltage v(z, t) and current i(z, t) at its input and v(z + Δz, t), i(z + Δz, t) at its output.
Kirchhoff's voltage law round the series path and Kirchhoff's current law at the shunt node give
answer.pre:
v(z, t) − RΔz i(z, t) − LΔz ∂i/∂t − v(z + Δz, t) = 0
i(z, t) − GΔz v(z + Δz, t) − CΔz ∂v/∂t − i(z + Δz, t) = 0

answer.text: Divide by Δz and let Δz → 0. These are the telegrapher's equations; in phasor form (∂/∂t → jω) they become ordinary equations in z:
answer.pre:
∂v/∂z = −R i − L ∂i/∂t        ∂i/∂z = −G v − C ∂v/∂t
dV/dz = −(R + jωL) I          dI/dz = −(G + jωC) V

answer.text: Differentiate the first phasor equation and substitute the second:
answer.pre:
d²V/dz² = −(R + jωL) dI/dz = (R + jωL)(G + jωC) V = γ² V
γ = α + jβ = √((R + jωL)(G + jωC))

answer.text: The general solution is a forward and a backward wave. Putting it into dV/dz = −(R + jωL)I gives the current, and the ratio of voltage to current of the forward wave is Z0:
answer.pre:
V(z) = V⁺e<sup>−γz</sup> + V⁻e<sup>γz</sup>
I(z) = (V⁺e<sup>−γz</sup> − V⁻e<sup>γz</sup>) / Z0
Z0 = (R + jωL)/γ = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC))

answer: Units and meaning: α in Np/m sets how fast the wave shrinks (8.686 dB per neper), β in rad/m sets the wavelength λ = 2π/β and the phase velocity vp = ω/β, and Z0 is in ohms. The minus sign on the backward current means that wave carries current the other way.
Lossless limits: with R = G = 0, Z0 = √(L/C) is real, α = 0, β = ω√(LC) and vp = 1/√(LC). For a low-loss line α ≈ R/(2Z0) + GZ0/2.

answer.text: Closing check with numbers (the line of the line-parameters chapter at 10 MHz):

answer: So the line has Z0 ≈ 50 Ω, loses 0.0109 dB per metre, and has λ = 2π/0.3142 = 20.0 m at 10 MHz, which agrees with vp = ω/β = 2.0×10⁸ m/s.

bank.q: What is waveform distortion on a line? Derive the condition for a distortionless line and explain how loading coils approximate it.
outline: Distortion = different frequencies attenuated differently and travelling at different speeds, so a pulse spreads
α = Re(γ) depends on ω in general; β/ω also varies, giving dispersion
Distortionless condition R/L = G/C
Then α = √(RG) independent of ω and vp = 1/√(LC) independent of ω
Loading adds series inductance L to bring R/L down towards G/C
Remark that this works for audio pairs, not for microwave lines
answer: Distortion. A pulse is a sum of sinusoids. It keeps its shape only if every component is attenuated by the same factor and delayed by the same time. On a general line α = Re γ depends on ω (amplitude distortion) and β is not proportional to ω, so vp = ω/β changes with frequency (phase or delay distortion). The pulse arrives smeared.

answer.text: Factor L and C out of γ²:
answer.pre: γ² = (R + jωL)(G + jωC) = LC (R/L + jω)(G/C + jω)

answer.text: If R/L = G/C = k, the two brackets are equal and the square root is exact:
answer.pre:
γ = √(LC) (k + jω)
α = k√(LC) = R√(C/L) = √(RG)      (independent of ω)
β = ω√(LC)                          (proportional to ω)
vp = ω/β = 1/√(LC)                  (independent of ω)

answer.text: The characteristic impedance is real and constant too:

answer: So the distortionless condition is R/L = G/C (equivalently RC = LG). Every frequency is attenuated by e<sup>−αl</sup> with the same α and arrives after the same delay l√(LC); the pulse shrinks but keeps its shape.

Why loading coils. In a real telephone pair R/L is much larger than G/C (copper resistance is large, leakage is tiny). Lowering R is costly, and raising G adds loss, so instead L is raised: loading coils are series inductors inserted at regular intervals, which raise the average L per metre and bring R/L down towards G/C.

answer.text: Numerical check with the line R = 0.1 Ω/m, L = 0.25 µH/m, G = 10 µS/m, C = 100 pF/m:

answer: Remark: loading works for audio-band pairs, where lumped coils every kilometre or so look continuous to the signal. It is not used on microwave lines, where the coils would themselves be electrically long; there, low-loss dielectrics and wide conductors keep α small instead.
Check: with L = 1.0 µH/m, R√(C/L) = 0.1 × √(10⁻¹⁰/10⁻⁶) = 0.1 × 0.01 = 0.0010 Np/m and G√(L/C) = 10⁻⁵ × 100 = 0.0010 Np/m. The two forms of α agree, as they must when R/L = G/C.

bank.q: Define reflection coefficient, VSWR and return loss for a line terminated in Z<sub>L</sub>. Derive the relations between them and state the values for open, short and matched loads.
outline: Γ = (Z<sub>L</sub> − Z₀)/(Z<sub>L</sub> + Z₀), generally complex
|Γ| ≤ 1; Γ = +1 open, −1 short, 0 matched
With d from the load, V(d) = V⁺(e<sup>jβd</sup> + ΓL e<sup>−jβd</sup>); adjacent maxima λ/2 apart, a maximum and the next minimum λ/4 apart
Return loss = −20 log|Γ| dB; matched gives infinite return loss
Power delivered to load = incident power × (1 − |Γ|²)

answer.text: Reflection coefficient. At the load the voltage and current are the sum of an incident wave V⁺ and a reflected wave V⁻. The load forces V/I = ZL, while each wave alone has V/I = ±Z0:

answer: ΓL is complex in general. For a passive load |ΓL| ≤ 1. At a distance d from the load towards the generator, Γ(d) = ΓL e<sup>−j2βd</sup>: on a lossless line only its phase turns.

answer.text: Standing wave and VSWR. With d measured from the load,

answer: The maximum |V⁺|(1 + |Γ|) occurs where the two waves are in phase and the minimum |V⁺|(1 − |Γ|) where they are opposite. Adjacent maxima are λ/2 apart; a maximum and the next minimum are λ/4 apart. So VSWR S = Vmax/Vmin = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), and inverting, |Γ| = (S − 1)/(S + 1).

Return loss. The reflected power is |Γ|² of the incident power, so RL = −10 log10|Γ|² = −20 log10|Γ| dB; it is positive, and a larger value means a better match. The power delivered is P⁺(1 − |Γ|²), and the mismatch loss is −10 log10(1 − |Γ|²) dB.

answer.text: Special loads:
Worked check, 50 Ω line and ZL = 100 + j50 Ω:

answer: Where the extremes sit: a maximum needs θ − 2βd = 0. With θ = 26.57° the first maximum is at d = (26.57°/720°)λ = 0.037λ from the load and the first minimum λ/4 further on, at 0.287λ. At a maximum the line impedance is real and equal to Z0 × S = 131 Ω; at a minimum it is Z0/S = 19.1 Ω. Measuring S and the position of a minimum is the classic slotted-line way to find an unknown load.
Check the inverse relation: |Γ| = (2.62 − 1)/(2.62 + 1) = 1.62/3.62 = 0.447, the value we started from.

bank.q: Explain TE and TM modes in a rectangular waveguide. Derive the cutoff frequency of the TE₁₀ mode and explain why it is called the dominant mode.
outline: TE: E<sub>z</sub> = 0, H<sub>z</sub> ≠ 0; TM: H<sub>z</sub> = 0, E<sub>z</sub> ≠ 0; TEM cannot exist in a single-conductor hollow guide
Boundary conditions give kc² = (mπ/a)² + (nπ/b)²
TE₁₀ has the lowest fc = c/2a for a > b
Below fc, γ is real, the wave decays as e<sup>−αz</sup>, no real power flows
Sketch the field pattern and the surface current on the broad wall
answer: Modes. Inside a hollow guide of broad wall a and narrow wall b the fields must satisfy Maxwell's equations and make the tangential E zero on the walls. Only discrete patterns fit. TE (transverse electric) modes have Ez = 0 and Hz ≠ 0; TM (transverse magnetic) modes have Hz = 0 and Ez ≠ 0. TEM cannot exist, because it needs two separate conductors at different potentials.

answer.text: For TE modes solve the wave equation for Hz with fields varying as e<sup>−γz</sup>:
answer.pre:
∂²Hz/∂x² + ∂²Hz/∂y² + kc² Hz = 0,     kc² = γ² + k²,   k = ω√(με)
Hz = H0 cos(mπx/a) cos(nπy/b) e<sup>−γz</sup>

answer: The cosines are forced by the walls: Ey ∝ ∂Hz/∂x must vanish at x = 0 and x = a, and Ex ∝ ∂Hz/∂y at y = 0 and y = b. So kx = mπ/a and ky = nπ/b, with m, n = 0, 1, 2, … but not both zero.

answer.text: The propagation constant then follows:

answer: If k < kc, γ is real: the field decays as e<sup>−αz</sup> and no real power flows (evanescent). If k > kc, γ = jβ is imaginary and the mode propagates. The boundary k = kc is cutoff:

answer.text: TE10: m = 1, n = 0 gives fc10 = c/(2a). Its only field components are Ey, Hx and Hz, with Ey = E0 sin(πx/a): zero at the side walls and largest at the centre, the same at every height y.

svg.aria: TE10 electric field across a rectangular guide cross-section with its sine profile

answer: Why dominant. With a > b, every other mode has a larger kc: TE20 has 2π/a, TE01 has π/b > π/a, and TM modes need m, n ≥ 1, so TM11 has √((π/a)² + (π/b)²). TE10 therefore has the lowest cutoff and is the only mode between fc10 and the next cutoff, so a guide used in that band carries one known pattern with one λg and one wave impedance.

Surface current. Js = n̂ × H. On the broad walls the current has a transverse part that is zero at the centre line x = a/2, so a narrow longitudinal slot there cuts no current and does not radiate; that is how slotted measuring lines work.

answer.text: Numbers for the standard X-band guide, a = 2.286 cm, b = 1.016 cm:

answer: Check: the single-mode band is 6.56 to 13.12 GHz, a 2 : 1 range because b < a/2 keeps TE01 above TE20; at 10 GHz λg = 3 cm/√(1 − 0.656²) = 3.98 cm.

bank.q: A 50 Ω lossless line of length 0.3λ is terminated in Z<sub>L</sub> = 100 + j50 Ω. Calculate the reflection coefficient at the load, the VSWR, and the input impedance.
outline: Γ<sub>L</sub> = (Z<sub>L</sub> − Z₀)/(Z<sub>L</sub> + Z₀), compute magnitude and angle in complex form
|Γ| from the result; S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|)
βl = 2π × 0.3 = 0.6π rad, tan βl evaluated correctly
Use Z<sub>in</sub> = Z₀(Z<sub>L</sub> + jZ₀ tan βl)/(Z₀ + jZ<sub>L</sub> tan βl)
Alternatively rotate Γ<sub>L</sub> by −2βl and convert back
State units (Ω) and that the answer is complex
answer: Data: Z0 = 50 Ω, ZL = 100 + j50 Ω, l = 0.3λ, lossless.

answer.text: Reflection coefficient at the load:

answer: VSWR: S = (1 + 0.447)/(1 − 0.447) = 1.447/0.553 = 2.62. Return loss −20 log10 0.447 = 6.99 dB (asked only as a check of the match).
Electrical length: βl = 2π × 0.3 = 0.6π rad = 108°, so tan βl = tan 108° = −3.078. Keep the calculator in radians if you enter 0.6π = 1.885.

answer.text: Input impedance by formula, Zin = Z0(ZL + jZ0 tan βl)/(Z0 + jZL tan βl):
Second route, rotating Γ (the Smith-chart method in numbers): moving 0.3λ towards the generator turns Γ by 2βl = 216°.

answer: Interpretation: the input looks like 19.2 Ω in series with a small inductive reactance of 3.5 Ω. Being near the real axis and below Z0, the point sits close to a voltage minimum: a minimum lies at 0.287λ, only 0.013λ from the input.

On the Smith chart the same result is a turn of 0.3λ clockwise: zL = 2 + j1 reads 0.213λ on the wavelengths-toward-generator scale, so the input reads 0.213λ + 0.300λ = 0.513λ, which is 0.013λ past the left-hand end of the real axis. The point is just above the axis near r = 0.38, giving zin ≈ 0.38 + j0.07, the same as the formula.
Check: |Γin| = √(0.441² + 0.0733²) = 0.447, the same as at the load, as it must be on a lossless line; and Zin is complex, with units of ohms.

bank.q: Design a quarter-wave transformer to match a 200 Ω resistive load to a 50 Ω line at 2 GHz on an air-spaced line. Find the section impedance and its physical length, and state the bandwidth limitation.
outline: l = λ/4 with λ = c/f = 0.15 m, so l = 37.5 mm
The match is exact at f₀ (and 3f₀, 5f₀ for the ideal section); reflection grows away from f₀, VSWR ≤ 1.5 from 1.65 to 2.35 GHz
Bandwidth widens for smaller impedance ratio
Mention that the load must be real; otherwise a stub must first cancel reactance
answer: Data: Z0 = 50 Ω, RL = 200 Ω (real), f0 = 2 GHz, air-spaced line so vp = c = 3×10⁸ m/s.

answer.text: Section impedance: the λ/4 section turns RL into Z0′²/RL, which must equal Z0.
Physical length:

answer: Check at f0: Zin = 100²/200 = 50 Ω, a perfect match.

answer.text: Bandwidth: away from f0 the section is not 90° long. The input |Γ| was computed from Zin = 100(200 + j100 tan θ)/(100 + j200 tan θ), θ = (π/2)(f/f0):
The same band from the bandwidth formula, with Γm = 0.2:

answer: So VSWR ≤ 1.5 holds from 1.65 to 2.35 GHz, 35 % of f0. A 2 : 1 ratio would give 78 %; the 4 : 1 ratio here halves it. The ideal section also matches again at 3f0 = 6 GHz.

Why a 4 : 1 ratio is narrower: the further ZL is from Z0, the larger the reflection the section has to undo, so a given error in electrical length leaves a larger |Γ|. Building it: in air coax a 100 Ω section needs ln(b/a) = 100/60 = 1.667, so b/a = 5.29; in microstrip it is a narrower strip than the 50 Ω line.

Limitations: the load must be real (cancel any reactance first with a stub or a length of line), the section impedance must be realisable (100 Ω is fine in coax or microstrip), and for wider bands use two or more λ/4 sections with stepped impedances (binomial or Chebyshev) or a taper.
Check: the band edges are f0(1 ∓ 0.351/2) = 2 × 0.8245 = 1.649 GHz and 2 × 1.1755 = 2.351 GHz, and the table gives |Γ| = 0.200 at both, agreeing with the formula.

bank.q: A 50 Ω line feeds a load of 25 + j40 Ω at 1 GHz. Using the Smith chart, find the position and length of a single short-circuited shunt stub that matches the line. Take an air-spaced line and check the answer by formula.
outline: Normalize z<sub>L</sub> = 0.5 + j0.8 and plot it
Rotate towards the generator to the g = 1 circle (or the 1 + jb circle) and read the distance d in wavelengths
Read the susceptance b at that point and convert to admittance
Stub susceptance must be −b; locate the short (y = ∞) and move along the outer circle
Read stub length ls in wavelengths, convert to metres with λ = c/f
Note the two possible solutions and the physical realizability check
answer: Data: Z0 = 50 Ω, ZL = 25 + j40 Ω, f = 1 GHz. Take an air-spaced line, so λ = c/f = 30 cm (on another line use λ = vp/f).

Normalise: zL = (25 + j40)/50 = 0.5 + j0.8. Plot it where the r = 0.5 circle meets the x = +0.8 arc. Γ = (zL − 1)/(zL + 1) = 0.555∠93.9°, so the VSWR circle has radius 0.555 and cuts the right-hand real axis at r = 3.49 = VSWR.

A shunt stub adds admittance, so go to admittance: yL is the point diametrically opposite zL on the VSWR circle, yL = 1/zL = 0.562 − j0.899. Its reading on the wavelengths-toward-generator (WTG) scale is 0.370λ.

Move clockwise (towards the generator) along the VSWR circle to the g = 1 circle. The first crossing is y = 1 + j1.334 at WTG 0.172λ. Distance: 0.500λ − 0.370λ = 0.130λ to the end of the scale, then 0.172λ more, so d1 = 0.302λ.

At that point the line admittance is 1 + j1.334, so the stub must supply −j1.334. The short-circuit point on the admittance chart is y = ∞ at the right-hand end (WTG 0.250λ). Move clockwise along the outer circle (g = 0) to b = −1.334, which reads WTG 0.352λ: ls1 = 0.352λ − 0.250λ = 0.102λ.

bank.q: A microstrip line is built on a 0.8 mm thick substrate with εr = 4.4 and copper strip width 1.5 mm. Find Z₀, ε<sub>eff</sub> and the guided wavelength at 5 GHz, and state why closed-form formulas are only approximate.
outline: Compute W/h = 1.875; use a microstrip synthesis/analysis formula or a chart
ε<sub>eff</sub> = (εr + 1)/2 + (εr − 1)/2 × 1/√(1 + 12h/W), giving a value between 1 and εr
Z₀ falls as W/h rises and as ε<sub>eff</sub> rises
λg = λ₀/√ε<sub>eff</sub>, with λ₀ = 60 mm at 5 GHz
Formulas are curve fits to quasi-static solutions; fringing fields, dispersion and finite strip thickness are ignored
Confirm with a field solver or measurement
answer: Data: εr = 4.4, h = 0.8 mm, W = 1.5 mm, f = 5 GHz.
Step 1, the ratio: W/h = 1.5/0.8 = 1.875 ≥ 1, so the wide-strip formulas apply. Only the ratio enters, so this line has the same εeff and Z0 as the 3 mm strip on 1.6 mm in the printed-lines chapter.

answer.text: Step 2, effective permittivity:
Step 3, characteristic impedance:
Step 4, guided wavelength at 5 GHz:
Summary of the working:

answer: Why the formulas are approximate: they are curve fits to quasi-static (low-frequency) field solutions, accurate to about one per cent within their range. They ignore the strip thickness, dispersion (εeff rises towards εr as frequency rises, so λg shrinks a little at 5 GHz), conductor roughness and the spread of εr in a cheap substrate, and they hold only for their W/h range (a separate pair is used below W/h = 1).

answer.text: Step 5, the width for exactly 50 Ω from the synthesis formula (valid for W/h < 2):

answer: So a 1.53 mm strip gives 50 Ω; the 1.5 mm strip is 0.03 mm too narrow, which is the 0.8 Ω excess. In practice the first design comes from these formulas, then a field solver or a test coupon on the real board confirms Z0 and λg.
Check: εeff = 3.32 lies between 1 and 4.4 as it must, and 50.8 Ω is just above 50 Ω because W/h = 1.875 is a little below the 1.91 needed for 50 Ω.

bank.q: A rectangular cavity resonator is 30 mm × 15 mm × 20 mm, air filled with copper walls (σ = 5.8×10⁷ S/m), and operates in the TE₁₀₁ mode. Calculate its resonant frequency and unloaded Q, and its bandwidth when unloaded and when critically coupled.
outline: Resonant frequency f = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (p/d)²) for TE₁₀ₚ with length d; f₁₀₁ = 9.01 GHz
Rs = √(πfμ₀/σ) for copper
Q₀ = ω₀ × stored energy / power lost, from the TE₁₀ₚ formula; about 9180
Q falls as Rs rises (higher frequency, rougher surface)
Loaded Q includes external coupling and is lower than unloaded Q
Bandwidth BW = f₀/Q<sub>L</sub>
answer: Data: a = 30 mm, b = 15 mm, d = 20 mm, air filled, TE101. Take copper walls, σ = 5.8×10⁷ S/m.

answer.text: Resonant frequency: the cavity is a guide closed at both ends, so f = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (n/b)² + (p/d)²) with m = 1, n = 0, p = 1:

answer: Is TE101 the lowest mode? With b the smallest side, the TE10p and TM110 family is lowest; TM110 would need (1/a)² + (1/b)² = 1111 + 4444, larger, so yes, TE101 is the dominant cavity mode.

answer.text: Surface resistance and wave number:
Unloaded Q from the stored energy and the wall loss (the TE10p result, worked in centimetres):
answer.pre: Q0 = (kad)³ b η / (2π² Rs) × 1/(2p²a³b + 2bd³ + p²a³d + ad³)

answer: Meaning: Q0 = ω0 × (stored energy)/(power lost in the walls). Q0 rises with the volume-to-surface ratio and falls as Rs rises; Rs grows as √f and with surface roughness, so a rough or plated surface gives less than this ideal value.
Loaded Q: coupling into and out of the cavity adds external loss, 1/QL = 1/Q0 + 1/Qe, so QL < Q0. Critically coupled (Qe = Q0) the loaded Q is 4590.
Bandwidth: BW = f0/QL. Unloaded, 9.014 GHz/9180 = 0.98 MHz; critically coupled, 1.96 MHz.

Check: the result is of the order of several thousand, as expected for an air-filled copper cavity at X band, and close to the 7820 found in the resonator chapter for a slightly smaller cavity at 9.97 GHz.

bank.q: Compare microstrip, stripline and coplanar waveguide for a 10 GHz front end. Discuss loss, radiation, dispersion, fabrication and the ease of mounting shunt components.
outline: Field picture of each: microstrip half-air half-dielectric, stripline fully buried, CPW both conductors on one face
Microstrip is open, so it radiates at bends and discontinuities and is quasi-TEM and dispersive; stripline is shielded, pure TEM and non-dispersive
CPW keeps ground close, so shunt parts mount without vias; microstrip needs vias
Fabrication: all are etched on PCB or thin film; stripline needs bonding of layers
Dispersion and higher-order modes set an upper frequency for each
Choose: microstrip for cheap mixed-signal boards, stripline for shielded low-loss runs, CPW for mm-wave MMICs
answer: The three lines differ in where their field sits, and every other difference follows from that.

answer.text: Field picture and type of wave:

head: Line
Field
Wave
εeff
rows: between strip and ground, partly in air above
between strip and two grounds, all in dielectric
across the gaps between centre strip and side grounds on one face

answer: Numbers at 10 GHz on εr = 4.4: λ0 = 30 mm. For the microstrip of the printed-lines chapter (W/h = 1.875) εeff = 3.32 and λg = 30/1.823 = 16.5 mm; in stripline εeff = 4.4 and λg = 30/2.098 = 14.3 mm; in CPW roughly 30/√2.7 = 18.3 mm. A quarter wave is 3.6 to 4.6 mm, so every bend and stub matters.

Loss: conductor loss rises with √f in all three. Microstrip and CPW have part of the field in air, so slightly less dielectric loss than stripline for the same substrate, but stripline's fields are shielded. Dielectric loss rises in proportion to f and tan δ.

Radiation: microstrip and CPW are open, so bends, steps and open ends radiate, and the loss grows with frequency and substrate thickness. Stripline is enclosed by two grounds and hardly radiates, which also gives good isolation between neighbouring lines.
Dispersion: microstrip and CPW are quasi-TEM, so εeff and Z0 change with frequency; stripline is pure TEM and does not disperse, apart from the dielectric itself.

Fabrication: microstrip is a single etched layer on a two-sided board, the cheapest. Stripline needs a multilayer board with the strip bonded between two grounds and vias to tie them. CPW is a single layer but needs narrow, accurate gaps.

Mounting shunt parts: in CPW the ground is beside the strip on the same face, so a shunt capacitor or transistor is soldered straight across the gap. Microstrip needs a via through the substrate to reach ground, which adds inductance (about a nanohenry, j63 Ω at 10 GHz). Stripline parts must sit on an outer layer and reach the strip through vias.

Recommendation for a 10 GHz front end: microstrip for most of the board (cheap, easy to tune, components on top), CPW where many shunt parts or an MMIC with ground-signal-ground pads sit, and stripline for long buried runs or feed networks that need shielding and isolation.
Check: the three λg values, 14.3, 16.5 and 18.3 mm, are ordered by εeff exactly as the field pictures predict.

bank.q: Explain how the Smith chart is constructed from the reflection-coefficient plane, and show how line rotation, VSWR and matching appear on it.
outline: Γ = |Γ|e<sup>jθ</sup>; the chart is the unit circle of |Γ| ≤ 1
Substitute Γ = (z − 1)/(z + 1) to get constant-r and constant-x circles
Constant r circles centred on the real axis, constant x arcs from the right-hand point
Lossless line movement = clockwise rotation by 2βl at constant |Γ|, half a turn per λ/2
VSWR = value of r at the positive real-axis crossing of the |Γ| circle
Matching: move to g = 1, then add a stub of the right susceptance
Limits: the chart is lossless and single frequency; lossy lines spiral inwards

answer.text: The Γ plane. For a line of real Z0, every normalised load z = Z/Z0 = r + jx has a reflection coefficient Γ = (z − 1)/(z + 1) = u + jv. A passive load has |Γ| ≤ 1, so all of them lie inside the unit circle. Inverting:
Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator and separate real and imaginary parts:
Constant-r circles: rearrange the first equation and complete the square:

answer: So each r value is a circle with centre (r/(1 + r), 0) on the real axis and radius 1/(1 + r). r = 0 is the outer circle, r = 1 passes through the centre, and every circle touches the point Γ = +1.

answer.text: Constant-x circles from the second equation:

answer: Each x value is a circle with centre (1, 1/x) and radius 1/|x|; only the arc inside the unit circle is drawn. Positive x (inductive) is in the upper half, negative x (capacitive) in the lower half. All arcs pass through Γ = +1, the open circuit; Γ = −1 is the short, and the centre Γ = 0 is the match z = 1.

Line rotation: on a lossless line Γ(d) = ΓL e<sup>−j2βd</sup>, so moving a distance d towards the generator keeps |Γ| and turns the point clockwise by 2βd. A full turn is d = λ/2, and λ/4 is half a turn, which is why the outer scale is marked in wavelengths towards the generator (WTG), 0 to 0.5λ.

VSWR: points with the same |Γ| lie on a circle centred on the chart centre. Where it cuts the positive real axis, Γ = |Γ| is real, so z = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|) = r = VSWR: the VSWR is read directly as the r value there.

Admittance: y = 1/z corresponds to −Γ, the point diametrically opposite, so the same chart read as g and b serves for admittance. A shunt-stub match is then: plot zL, take yL opposite, rotate clockwise on the VSWR circle to the g = 1 circle, and add a stub of susceptance −b.

answer.text: Example drawn to scale in the Smith-chart chapter, 100 + j50 Ω on 50 Ω:

answer: Limits: the chart assumes one frequency and one real Z0. On a lossy line the point spirals inwards, |Γ| falling by e<sup>−2αd</sup>, rather than staying on a circle. Accuracy is that of the drawing, about two figures; modern instruments and CAD tools plot the same chart on screen.
Check: the r = 1 circle has centre (0.5, 0) and radius 0.5, so it passes through the centre and through Γ = +1, exactly the g = 1 circle used for matching.

bank.q: Discuss the high-frequency effects that make the simple R, L, G, C model break down, and explain how they change the choice of matching method and its bandwidth.
outline: Skin effect raises R with √f; proximity effect adds more
Dielectric loss makes G rise with frequency; tan δ of the substrate
Dispersion: ε<sub>eff</sub> and Z₀ vary with frequency on microstrip
Radiation and surface waves at higher frequencies
Component parasitics: lead inductance, pad capacitance, so lumped matching fails above a few GHz
Distributed matching (stubs, tapers) preferred; narrowband vs broadband trade-off; the Bode–Fano limit bounds match quality over a band
Measure with a VNA and S-parameters rather than assuming the model
answer: The R, L, G, C model treats the four constants as fixed numbers. At high frequency each of them changes, and new effects appear that the model does not contain.

answer.text: Skin effect: current crowds into a surface layer of depth δs = √(2/(ωμσ)), so R rises as √f. For copper (σ = 5.8×10⁷ S/m):

answer: Proximity effect and surface roughness add more: when δs falls below the roughness of the copper, the current path lengthens and R rises further.

answer.text: Dielectric loss: G = ωC tan δ, so G rises in proportion to f. For C = 100 pF/m, Z0 = 50 Ω and a good dielectric with tan δ = 0.0004:

answer: Dispersion: on microstrip and CPW the wave is quasi-TEM, so εeff, Z0 and vp change with frequency; a line designed with the static formulas drifts in electrical length at high frequency.

Radiation and higher modes: open lines radiate at bends and discontinuities, and above a certain frequency surface waves and higher-order modes appear, so the line no longer carries a single TEM-like wave.

answer.text: Parasitics of lumped parts: a component lead or via of about 1 nH and a pad of about 0.5 pF already matter at a few gigahertz:

answer: Effect on the choice of matching. Lumped L-C matching works up to roughly a gigahertz or two, where the parasitics stay small next to the reactances needed. Above that, distributed matching (quarter-wave sections, stubs, tapers) is preferred, because its "components" are lengths of line whose behaviour is predictable.

Effect on bandwidth. Every simple match is narrowband: a single quarter-wave section keeps VSWR ≤ 1.5 over 78 % for a 2 : 1 ratio but only 35 % for 4 : 1, and a single stub is narrower still because its reactance changes with frequency. Wider bands need multi-section transformers, tapers or double stubs. The Bode–Fano limit sets a ceiling: a load that stores energy (a reactive load) cannot be matched to a low |Γ| over an arbitrarily wide band by any lossless network.
In practice the design is checked by measurement: a vector network analyser gives S11 (Γ) and S21 across the band, and the model is adjusted to the measured R(f), G(f) and εeff(f).
Check: Rs scales as √f, so from 1 GHz to 10 GHz it should grow by √10 = 3.16: 8.3 mΩ × 3.16 = 26 mΩ, as in the table; and αd grows ten times, 0.055 to 0.55 dB/m.

bank.q: A 28 GHz link must carry 1 W. Recommend a transmission medium and a matching approach, justifying the choice against waveguide, coaxial line and printed microstrip.
outline: Waveguide: lowest loss per metre at mm-wave, high power handling, bulky, cut off below fc
Coax: convenient up to about 20 GHz; losses and connector repeatability hurt at 28 GHz
Microstrip: compact, integrates with the radio chip, but loss, radiation and tight tolerance at 28 GHz
Compare attenuation in dB/m, power handling, size and cost
Matching: waveguide iris or stub for the antenna feed, printed stub or taper on the board
Note bandwidth required by 1 W and linearity, plus mechanical alignment tolerance
answer: Requirement: carry 1 W at 28 GHz from the radio to the antenna with low loss. 1 W is a small power for every medium below, so the choice is set by loss, size and integration, not by breakdown.

answer.text: Waveguide. The standard guide for this band (WR-28) is a = 7.112 mm, b = 3.556 mm:
Its copper wall loss from the TE10 attenuation formula αc = Rs(2bπ² + a³k²)/(a³bβkη), with Rs = 0.0437 Ω:
Coaxial line. Take a 50 Ω air-filled coax of outer radius 1.46 mm and inner radius 0.635 mm (b/a = 2.3), the best case for a coax of this size:
answer.pre:
αc = Rs (1/a + 1/b) / (2η ln(b/a)) = 0.0437 × 2260 / (2 × 377 × 0.833) = 0.157 Np/m = 1.37 dB/m
first higher mode (TE11) cutoff ≈ c/(π(a + b)) = 45.6 GHz, so 28 GHz is single-mode

answer: A real flexible cable has a solid dielectric, a smaller inner conductor for the same Z0 and connector losses, so it is worse than this best case, and repeatability of connectors becomes an issue at 28 GHz.

answer.text: Microstrip. A 50 Ω line on a thin low-loss board, εr = 3.5, h = 0.25 mm, tan δ = 0.004: the synthesis formula gives W/h = 2.26, W = 0.56 mm, εeff = 2.75. Using the usual estimates αc ≈ Rs/(Z0W) and αd = k0εr(εeff − 1)tanδ/(2√εeff(εr − 1)):
answer.pre:
αc ≈ 0.0437 / (50 × 0.000565) = 1.54 Np/m = 13.4 dB/m
αd = 1.73 Np/m = 15.0 dB/m
total ≈ 28 dB/m, that is about 2.8 dB per 10 cm

answer.text: Comparison for a 30 cm run:

head: Medium
Loss per metre
Loss in 30 cm
Size and integration
rows: flexible if cabled, connectors add loss
on the board, next to the chip

answer: Recommendation: keep the microstrip runs on the board to a few centimetres, just from the radio chip to a transition, and carry the signal to the antenna in waveguide (lowest loss, single-mode, shielded). Use coax only for short flexible links in test or where the antenna must move.

Matching approach: on the board use a printed quarter-wave section or a short open stub to match the chip to 50 Ω, since these are etched with the line and need no parts; at the waveguide use a microstrip-to-waveguide probe transition tuned with a back-short about λg/4 behind the probe (about 4.1 mm here) and, if needed, an inductive iris to cancel the remaining susceptance. Check the match over the whole channel bandwidth, since all these are narrowband.
Other factors: 28 GHz parts need tight mechanical tolerance (a λg/4 of 4.1 mm means a 0.1 mm error is about 2° of phase), and linearity of the 1 W amplifier matters more than the line's power rating.
Check: 0.67 dB/m × 0.3 m = 0.20 dB and 28.4 dB/m × 0.3 m = 8.5 dB, so the waveguide saves about 8 dB, nearly a factor of seven in power, over the same run.

glossary.def: A pair of conductors, or a conductor over a ground plane, that guides a wave from source to load.
Per-metre values R, L, G and C that describe a line whose length is comparable with a wavelength.
The coupled first-order equations for voltage and current along a line.
The ratio of forward voltage to forward current on a line, Z₀ = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC)).
γ = α + jβ, the complex number giving attenuation and phase change per metre.
α, the real part of γ, in nepers per metre; it sets how fast the wave shrinks.
β, the imaginary part of γ, in radians per metre; it sets wavelength along the line.
The speed at which one frequency's phase travels, vp = ω/β.
The speed at which the envelope of a modulated signal travels, vg = dω/dβ.
A line with R/L = G/C, so all frequencies are attenuated equally and travel at the same speed.
Γ = (Z<sub>L</sub> − Z₀)/(Z<sub>L</sub> + Z₀), the complex ratio of reflected to incident voltage at the load.
A fixed pattern of voltage maxima and minima formed by forward and reflected waves.
Voltage standing wave ratio, S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), between 1 and infinity.
−20 log₁₀|Γ| in dB; the larger the value, the better the match.
Line length expressed as βl in radians or as a fraction of a wavelength.
The impedance seen looking into a line at a given distance from the load.
A short length of line, open or shorted, placed in shunt or series to cancel reactance.
A λ/4 line of impedance √(Z₀Z<sub>L</sub>) that matches a real load to a line at one frequency.
A polar chart of reflection coefficient on which normalized impedance and admittance are plotted.
A printed strip on one side of a dielectric slab with a ground plane on the other.
A printed strip buried between two ground planes in a dielectric.
A centre strip with ground strips on the same face of the substrate.
The permittivity a printed line behaves as if it had when its field is partly in air.
The frequency below which a waveguide mode cannot propagate.
The distance between phase fronts inside a waveguide, λg = λ₀/√(1 − (fc/f)²).
Q = ω₀ × stored energy ÷ lost power, which fixes a resonator's bandwidth.
The loss of delivered power caused by reflection, −10 log₁₀(1 − |Γ|²) dB.
The mode with the lowest cutoff frequency in a waveguide; TE₁₀ in a rectangular guide and TE₁₁ in a circular one.
Coupling at which the external Q equals the unloaded Q, so the loaded Q is half the unloaded Q and all power is absorbed at resonance.
